questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Ireland was not my first choice. Originally I'd been accepted to New Zealand, but had to cancel that trip as it wasn't possible to go on exchange in NZ in the fall of 2022.
When re-applying I was then left with choosing countries within Europe. I opted for a place that I hadn't seen before and that primarily spoke English and thus ended with choosing UCC in Ireland.
Originally I looked very much into what courses were available but when applying the second time it was more about finding a place that seemed to have a novel study atmosphere and would offer exciting experiences outside of academia. UCC luckily offers some very interesting courses in biology and zoology that I couldn't have taken back home, but this wasn't my main priority when choosing it.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was relatively easy. UCC does a good job of giving introductory lectures and making groups on social media for providing information, however I was introduced to most of it only when arriving, not before, and mainly by my roommates who'd been there a few days longer than me. It's a little chaotic, but overall you quickly get into the flow of thing and luckily UCC in general is very good at sharing and providing necessary information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The international office offered a number of orientation lectures as well as tours of the campus and even the city. The student union also hosted some outreach programs to assist international students and getting them acquainted with the workings of UCC. You could also contact anyone you needed though it could be difficult to get a reply by email in those first couple of weeks

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It wasn't super easy. Housing is both expensive and limited in Cork. Despite a lot of different student accomodations being offered, these fill up very quickly and you need to be out searching as soon as possible. I began looking in May and got rejected from pretty much every place that I inquired. A lot of student housing is associated with UCC through their housing program, but this is hardly available to international students as they only have a limited number available and to enter the lottery you need to apply with your student ID months before this is provided for internationals. 

There's also a lot of scammers in Ireland because the housing market is so dire, so one need to be on the lookout for that as well. I myself was in touch with a guy who offered to rent me a room pretty cheap, but he refused to call or have any further contact than by text. I know of a few students who'd made a downpayment on a rental only to show up and not be able to contact their "landlord" anymore, or even just get refused because they hadn't double-checked the legal validity of the contract they'd signed.

Luckily by reading another review like this I came upon Brookfield village. I'd never heard of it in my initial google searches, but when looking up the name it popped up. They luckily had room, and from what I can tell they typically don't fill up as early as many other places. It's also one of the cheaper options for students, and is only ten minutes further down College Road than the main campus. It's a little bit outside the city (about 20-30 minutes walk) and there isn't the best nearby grocery-options, but overall it's pretty nice. Granted the rooms are a little small, the buildings old and you typically share a bathroom with three other people, living eight people in an apartment with two bathrooms. But for one semester it's more than adequate and the apartments can be very cozy especially of you're lucky with your roommates. I lived exclusively with other internationals and all the surrounding apartments were inhabited by international students as well, so it was very easy to get to know a lot of people.

The booking system to Brookfield is a little old fashioned and they are not the best at sending confirmation and such, so you have to take quite a bit of initiative to ensure that you are in fact booked for a room, but luckily I didn't have any further issues with them.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
There are many options, and most are pretty expensive. You typically have the choice of either living near campus or near the city, though a few places also lies well outside the city and away from campus as well. 
Busses in Cork come and go as they please and are impossible to predict (don't trust route planner on google), but are luckily frequent enough that you'll rarely be left waiting more than 20 minutes between busses. You can also attempt to acquire a bike (in fact there are several low price options for this), but no efforts are made in Irish infrastructure to make biking pleasant so walking might honestly be the best alternative as the city isn't that big.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Working out the timetables for the modules is a nightmare! Unless you specifically apply for modules that are of the same year and within the same course there's a good chance you'll have modules that overlap and clash in your final timetable, which you'll then have to figure out all over again. 

Initially the timetables weren't even available so I just applied for the courses I found most interesting. It was only a few weeks before the semester started that the timetables were released and then I learned that several of my modules clashed.

Besides there was a few courses that should have been open to international students which then suddenly wasn't. Several classes also needed department confirmation which didn't come until three weeks or so into the semester, so for quite a long time I was taking classes that I hadn't officially been accepted into yet. Figuring out how to get all my required classes to get the total amount of ECTS needed for the semester was quite an effort and I received little to no help from UCC as they do not create timetables for students.

The best I can say of the registration progress is that the book of modules for visiting students is quite user friendly and it was pretty easy to get a good grasp of what modules within the different courses were available and what they were about.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Very little. I had to figure most of my planning out myself, and the international office couldn't tell me what classes were open for internationals and which wasn't.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got the two main ones that I'd wanted but only because I prioritized them when figuring out how to make my timetable work, and this was at the cost of other classes that I had chosen back home. Of the six courses I'd originally applied for I had to change out three of them.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
It's hard to predict what courses might clash with others. Prepare yourself for the risk that you propaply can't take all the ones you'd initially wanted and that you will have to spend quite some time after arriving figuring out how to get a full class calendar that works. 
If you want to make life easier for yourself the apply for modules of the same course and year (course is the initial two letters like ZY for zoology, and year is the first cipher so 2000, 2001, 2002 etc. for second year classes).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The Courses were very interesting and the teachers were usually great, though there is a general discourse among Irish students where they don't participate much in the classes which obviously makes it a struggle for the lectures to really engage with them. 
Besides I got the general feeling that expectations to student performance were lower even though the workload was higher. Generally though the level of the courses seemed on par with what I've experienced at my home university, especially if you make an effort to participate and engage with the lecturers.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
It was mostly similar though they have a lot more continuous assessment than we do at my home university, which means that I had to spend a lot more time writing essays and working on assignments than I'm used to. The biggest problem is that these aren't very well spread out as most teachers want to put the assignments only a few weeks before exams, so in the final weeks of the semester everyone is typically swarmed with assignments and personally I had about 80% of my assignments due in those last two weeks, with several of the details of several of them not having been released until just a week or two earlier. 
On the other hand the final exams were much much easier than anything I've tried back home.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
ZY3020: Animal behaviour
ZY3019: Adaptations to Extreme Environments
BL3004: Research Skills in Biology
PH3046: Philosophy of Biology
MB3005: The role and ecology of microbes in the environment
CC2250: Ancient Ireland

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Adaptations to extreme environments is very interesting and the final assignment is a big literature review that serves well to prepare for the bachelor thesis. 
Ancient Ireland is a great class if one is interested in learning a bit about medieval Irish history and Celtic culture.
I was pleasantly surprised by Research skills in biology and would recommend it for any biology student.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Alcohol and beer in the grocers are relatively expensive compared to Denmark. Travelling around the country is worth some research as especially between Cork and Dublin there is a variety of options that vary quite a bit in price. 
UCC offers free access to Mardyke Arena, a giant gym that has three gyms, a swimming pool, a climbing gym and many other facilities so no money has to be spend on such.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are a ton of clubs and societies to join at UCC, all of which has a calendar packed with activities and usually no obligations upon joining. I joined quite a few, but ended up mainly participating in one as that alone had so many activities that I was kept plenty busy in my free time.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The mountaneering club. They offer climbing sessions with instruction at Mardyke twice a week as well as a discount to the larger climbing gym in town once a week. They also do quite a few social events so you really can get to know them and everyone else in the club. I made more friends in this club than in my classes or through my accommodation. 

They also do weekly hiking trips every week which is a great and very cheap way to get to see a lot of Irelands nature (though pack hiking boots if you wish to join these). A lot of international students are in this club as well so there's a good chance of making both Irish and international friends.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: The hikes with the mountaneering club. Also join one or two of the longer trips that are arranged for international students, that visits some of Irelands most beautiful cities and sights such as the Ring of Kerry, Killarney, The Aran Islands, Galway and Belfast.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The culture is not too different from Danish culture so quite easy. The accent can be hard to interpret at times though

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join and particitate in a club or society

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The different aspect to studying, how Irish people generally seem to take it a lot less serious than I'm used to, which could be mildly frustrating.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The countryside, the history and the general welcoming hospitality of the people (though often with a bit of sarcasm and snark)

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Look for accomodation early and keep in mind where it is located, because living near campus or center is simply just very convenient. 

Be prepared that arranging you classes can and probably will be difficult

Make sure to join a club or society, they are a lot of fun and a great way to meet people, and there is something for everyone. It's also a good chance to learn something new.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: It rains more or less every day in Ireland. Bring waterproof clothes.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The many trips around the country, and interacting with the teachers who apparently are used to teaching very un-engaged student and got very excited whenever I would answer or ask a question

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Figuring out all the details in advance as I struggled to get all the paperwork both from my home-university and UCC

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
